caption: The three claims United Next rests on: hubs in seven of the largest premium markets, the only US carrier that retired no widebody type in the pandemic, and a ~30% gauge increase said to cut CASM-ex ~8% by 2026.

The 2018 mid-continent thesis in numbers: United's Chicago/Houston/Denver hubs ran 2.8 departures per spoke against 3.6-3.7 at Delta and American, 148 destinations against 165-167, and 16.8k connecting itineraries against 27.5-34.0k, producing a ~10-point margin gap to rival mid-continent hubs while international gateways ran ~7 points ahead.

How management frames the advantage: five pillars (global network, optimized fleet, leading product, best service, premier global carrier) with the whole plan resting on gauge correction rather than new destinations.
The demographic case for the hub map: United's metros rank at or near the top on total, international and premium passenger demand, which is the asserted source of premium pricing power.

Long-haul margin by entity against AA/DL in FY2019 from United's internal flight-profitability system: Pacific ~16 points, Atlantic ~9, Deep South America ~0, overall long-haul ~8. No filing discloses margin by region.
The starting gap: 104 seats per North American departure in July 2019 against 114 at AA/DL and 175 at the low-cost carriers, the lowest gauge among US majors.

Single-cabin regional jets ran 42% of United's Chicago departures against 28% for American at ORD, 19% at MSP and 18% at DTW; the plan cut ORD to ~4% and the system from 33% to ~10% by retiring 200+ 50-seaters.
Large narrowbodies (181+ seats) were 4% of United's narrowbody fleet in 2019 against 27% at AA/DL; United Next targeted ~33% by 2026, a 30-point move that depends on MAX 10 and A321neo deliveries.

United held 26% of small-city international traffic against 37% for AA/DL because 27% of Newark domestic departures ran on single-class regional jets against 13% for peers in New York; the plan took Newark to zero.
Bank scale: 10% of United's mid-continent hub banks had 70+ departures against 42% at AA/DL, with a target of 65% by 2026 achieved by upgauging inside existing gates rather than adding departures.
The gauge bridge that drives the whole plan: 104 seats per North American departure in 2019 to 109 in 2022 and ~134 in 2026. Management reported 126 at Q2-2026 against a restated 136-seat goal.
Premium seats per short-haul departure from 31 in 2019 to 39 in 2022 and 53 in 2026, a 75% increase, with premium capacity growing faster than main cabin.
Lie-flat seats per long-haul departure in 2019: United 44 against 32 at AA/DL (+40%) but 63 at the foreign-flag carriers serving United's hubs, so the premium-seat lead is over US rivals only.
The six structural gaps quantified: gauge +~30 seats, banks at critical mass 10% to 65%, mid-continent daily departures ~545 to ~650, frequencies per market +~10%, plus product and culture.
Where the 4-6% capacity CAGR was supposed to come from: 2-4 points of gauge, ~1 point of new routes and ~1 point of frequency. Realized 2019-2025 growth was 2.5% a year.

The revenue mix behind the plan: domestic economy cabin excluding Economy Plus was only 30% of 2019 revenue, falling to 27% by 2026, which is why the plan could assume TRASM ~1% below 2019 and still target 14% margins.
The $2bn structural cost program split $1.3bn workforce efficiency and $0.7bn non-labor, sized to offset inflation through 2023 on its own.
The aircraft-level unit economics claim: an A321neo seats ~55% more passengers than an A319 for ~13% more cost per departure, giving ~27% lower CASM-ex.
Incremental MAX 10 CASM-ex was put 48% below average domestic CASM-ex, letting United add capacity at a marginal unit cost below 6 cents.
Fuel cost per seat at a 700-mile stage: $36 on a 50-seat regional jet, $25 on an A319, $16 on a MAX 9, with the new fleet at least 50% more fuel-efficient per seat.

The CASM-ex waterfall: 10.21 cents in 2019 plus 0.8 of inflation, less 0.7 of structural savings and 0.5 of gauge to ~9.8 in 2023, then plus 0.6 of inflation, less 1.5 of gauge, plus 0.4 of stage length to ~9.4 in 2026. Actual 2025 CASM-ex was 12.64 cents.
The delivery schedule underwriting the plan: 40 aircraft in 2022, 138 in 2023 and 354 in 2024+, of which 186 MAX and 70 A321neo were newly ordered, supporting a 4.0-6.0% capacity CAGR through 2026.
The balance-sheet path: adjusted net debt $18bn in 2019 rising to $25bn through 2023 and back below $18bn by 2026, with leverage from 3.2x to below 2.5x. Net leverage reached 2.2x at YE2025.
United Next's full financial target table, including the 2026 fuel assumption of $2.20 a gallon that no transcript repeats; United paid $4.19 in Q2-2026.
Industry domestic revenue as a share of GDP: 0.71% in the 1990s, 0.54% in 2001-2010, 0.49% in 2011-2018 and 2019, with management's baseline assuming a return to ~0.49%.

The four supply constraints management said would keep industry capacity below plan: pilot demand of 10,000 against ~6,600 ATP issuances, sick rates 19% above 2H19, OEM delays, and airline and ATC technology.
Holiday 2022 cancellation rates as evidence of operating capability: Southwest 39%, Alaska 16%, Spirit 12%, Frontier 10%, Delta 7%, United 5%, JetBlue 4%, American 3%, at similar weather exposure.
United grew its widebody fleet 12% between YE2019 and YE2022 while AA/DL cut 9% and the leading global carriers cut 5%; it then flew 36% more Atlantic capacity than 2019 against 1% for the industry.

FY2022 CASM-ex against 2019 across eight US carriers: Frontier 29%, Spirit 22%, Southwest 20%, Alaska 19%, Delta 18%, United 15%, JetBlue 14%, American 12%, the cost-convergence chart behind the thesis that inflation passes through to fares.

The FY2023 guidance table issued the same day the United Next cost targets were abandoned: capacity up high teens, TRASM about flat, CASM-ex about flat including 4.5 points of labor, adjusted EPS $10-12.

Newark to Atlanta by departure, showing the regional-jet substitution as it happened in one market: United ran 8 frequencies at about 120 seats in 2004, 6 at about 57 seats in 2013, and 6 at about 137 seats in 2016, against Delta's 11 frequencies at about 134 seats. The gauge collapse United Next was still correcting in 2021 is dated here to the decade before.

United publishing the failure modes of its own revenue-management system: real unconstrained demand for a $526 Newark-Indianapolis fare is 12 passengers, Orion forecasts 1.8, and United therefore offers that fare only 15% of the time. The replacement system was sized at 1-2 points of PRASM and Kirby put the realised gain at 1.2 points a year later.

The 2016 cost plan: non-fuel unit cost up 3.5-4.5% in 2017 on labour resets, then under 1.0% a year through 2020, explicitly projected on 1.5% annual capacity growth. Capacity grew 3.5%, 4.9% and 3.5% instead, so the unit-cost target was met on a base three times larger than assumed.

The full $4.8bn earnings-initiative table by year and by line, with the column that appears nowhere else: how much of each initiative management judged unavailable to Delta, from ~100% for network and MileagePlus down to ~25% for segmentation. Pre-tax income in 2019 came in below 2015, the base year.

The plan's central promise in one waterfall: a (5.6)-point 2016 operating-margin gap to Delta closing through commercial, operational and cost improvements into a ~1.5-point premium by 2020. The gap was (4.1) points in 2019 and (1.2) in 2025, and all of the narrowing came from Delta's margin declining.

The per-mile economics both ways: a partner buys miles at $0.02 and the program buys the award seat back from United at $0.01, "a 50% profit", while miles earned by flying are sold to the program at a minimum $0.01 and bought back at cost. The footnote adds the contractual floor holding the United-related margin at 20% or better.

The cash-flow mechanics and the contract terms the financing forced into public view: monthly mile purchases from United under a 20-year operating agreement with a guaranteed 20% minimum margin, Chase and Visa co-brand agreements extended into 2029, 3-to-5-year terms for other partners, and redemption pricing set at the program's discretion.

Seven years of standalone loyalty EBITDA, $1,235m in 2014 to $1,882m for the twelve months to March 2020, against United's adjusted EBITDAR, and the ratio of miles issued to miles redeemed, 118% to 129% through the cycle and 140% as redemptions collapsed. This is the only published series for either measure.

MileagePlus as a standalone company: $5,330m of 2019 mile-sale cash split $3,803m third-party and $1,527m United, $1,938m of revenue net of redemptions, $110m of operating expense, $1,828m of EBITDA, $12,505m of assets and $6,161m of deferred revenue, which is $885m more than United's consolidated balance sheet deferred for the same program on the same date.

The stress case, run live: in April and May 2020 mile-sale collections halved while miles returned from cancelled flights exceeded miles redeemed by nearly 3x, turning redemption cost negative and lifting the program's net cash flow about 80% above the same two months of 2019. The loyalty business took in more cash as the airline stopped flying.

The United Next fleet targets restated unchanged in March 2022: 104 seats per short-haul North America departure to about 134 by 2026, premium seats from 31 to 53, and 2026 unit cost excluding fuel about 8% below 2019. This is the last dated document in which United presented that cost target as live.

The same deck's guidance page, two slides later: 2022 capacity down high single digits against 2019, first-quarter unit cost excluding fuel about 18% above 2019, and fuel at $2.99 a gallon against the $2.20 the 2026 target assumed. Every input to the plan restated on the previous page had already moved against it.
